e.etymology: A modern spelling of Lucy, from Lucia, the feminine of the Roman name Lucius, from Latin lux, light.

assoc.t: Luci, the demon in Netflix's Disenchantment

e.etymology: A Russian short form of Galina, from Greek galene, calm, and separately a Spanish feminine of Galo, from Latin Gallus. Gala Dalí, Salvador Dalí's wife and muse, made it known in the West.
namesakes: Gala Dalí (wife and muse of Salvador Dalí)

assoc.t: Gala apple, a common supermarket variety
gala, a formal party or benefit, as in the Met Gala

e.etymology: A spelling of Blaise, from the Roman name Blasius, probably from Latin blaesus, lisping. St Blaise was a 4th-century Armenian bishop; this spelling leans toward the word blaze.

assoc.t: blaze, the word for a strong fire (same sound)
to blaze, slang for smoking marijuana (same sound)

e.etymology: The name of the third book of the Bible, from Late Latin Leviticus and Greek Leuitikon, relating to the Levites, the priestly tribe of Levi. Parents use it as a long form of Levi.

assoc.t: Leviticus, the Bible's book of priestly law

e.etymology: A phonetic respelling of Naomi, from Hebrew No'omi, my pleasantness. In the Bible Naomi is the mother-in-law of Ruth.
From Arabic haniyya, the feminine of hani, happy or content. The name is widely used among Urdu speakers in Pakistan and India.
A Cuban name from the wave of newly made Y names popular on the island from the 1970s; it resembles the biblical Jasiel. Outfielder Yasiel Puig brought it to American attention.
namesakes: Yasiel Puig (Cuban outfielder for the Los Angeles Dodgers)

e.etymology: A name popular in Pakistan, usually linked to Arabic anaba, to turn back to God in repentance. It is not a classical Arabic name, and the meanings given in name lists vary.
From Ottoman Turkish, analyzed as or, fortress or city, plus han, khan or ruler. Orhan Gazi, the second Ottoman ruler, took Bursa in 1326 and made the name a Turkish standard.
namesakes: Orhan Pamuk (Turkish novelist, 2006 Nobel Prize in Literature)

e.meaning: a name of the goddess Durga
e.etymology: From Sanskrit Vamika, an epithet of the goddess Durga. It rose in use after Indian cricketer Virat Kohli and actress Anushka Sharma gave the name to their daughter in 2021.
From colleen, the Hiberno-English word for a girl, from Irish cailín. It is rare as a name in Ireland itself and took hold among Irish-descended families in America and Australia.
namesakes: Colleen Hoover (best-selling novelist of It Ends with Us)
Colleen McCullough (author of The Thorn Birds)

e.etymology: A spelling variant of Cody, from an Irish surname, an Anglicized form of Ó Cuidighthigh, descendant of the helpful one. Buffalo Bill Cody made the surname famous in America.
An English and Scottish surname from places named Crawford, from Old English crawe, crow, and ford, a river crossing.

assoc.t: surname of actress Joan Crawford and model Cindy Crawford

e.etymology: From the acacia tree, whose name comes through Latin from Greek akakia, probably from ake, a point or thorn. It joined other botanical names for girls in the late 20th century.

From Hebrew adin, delicate or gentle; in the Bible the sons of Adin return from exile with Ezra. Among Bosniaks a separate Adin comes from Arabic din, faith, and in the US it doubles as a spelling of Aden.
A respelling of Kenley with the -leigh ending. Kenley is an English surname and place name ending in Old English leah, a woodland clearing.
The English color word, a deep red, which came through Old Spanish and Medieval Latin from Arabic qirmizi, the dye made from the kermes insect.

assoc.t: Crimson Tide, the University of Alabama's sports teams
Harvard's school color and student newspaper

e.etymology: The Japanese word for the curved single-edged sword of the samurai, taken up as a girls' name in the United States. It is not used as a given name in Japan.

assoc.t: the katana, the samurai's curved sword
Katana, DC Comics swordswoman in Suicide Squad
Suzuki Katana motorcycle

e.meaning: scoundrel, one who breaks from the pack
e.etymology: The English word for a scoundrel or an independent rule-breaker, first recorded in the 1500s and of uncertain source. Rogue also exists as a surname that began as a nickname.

assoc.t: Rogue, the power-absorbing mutant of the X-Men
a rogue is a scoundrel; to go rogue is to defy the rules
Nissan Rogue SUV
Rogue One, the 2016 Star Wars film
Rogue Fitness gym equipment

e.note: The everyday word means a dishonest scoundrel as well as a free spirit.

e.etymology: In Arabic, the feminine of hani, happy or content, a name also common in Pakistan. In Polish, Hania is a pet form of Hanna, from Hebrew Channah, grace.
In Latvia Daila is a name tied to the word daiļš, beautiful. American use probably arose separately, alongside similar-sounding names such as Dayla, Dalia and Dahlia.
From Sanskrit nirvana, literally a blowing out: the release from desire and rebirth that is the goal of Buddhist and Hindu practice. Nirvaan is a common Indian spelling of the boys' name.
Usually treated as a form of Turkish Aysel, from ay, moon, and sel, stream or flood. This spelling is found mostly in South Asian Muslim families.
A modern Latin American spelling in the family of Zamira and Samira. Its recent rise in the US follows Venezuelan pop singer Zhamira Zambrano.

e.meaning: hill with a ledge, or steep-sided valley
e.etymology: An English surname from several places named Sheldon, from Old English scylf, shelf or ledge, with dun, hill, or denu, valley. It became a given name in the 19th century.
namesakes: Sheldon Cooper (physicist on The Big Bang Theory and Young Sheldon)
Sheldon Adelson (Las Vegas casino magnate and political donor)

assoc.t: Sheldon Cooper of The Big Bang Theory and Young Sheldon

e.note: Strongly tied to Sheldon Cooper, the socially awkward genius of The Big Bang Theory.

e.etymology: Two names share this spelling: Arabic samir, a companion in evening conversation, and Sanskrit samira, a breeze or gentle wind. It is used by Muslim and Hindu families alike.

e.meaning: one who has attained his goal
e.etymology: From Sanskrit siddhartha, built from siddha, accomplished, and artha, aim or purpose. Siddhartha Gautama was the birth name of the Buddha.
namesakes: Siddhartha Gautama (the Buddha, whose birth name this is)

e.etymology: Either the French word joie, joy, as in joie de vivre, or a spelling of Joey, the pet form of Josephine and Joseph. Both readings are in use.

assoc.t: joie de vivre, the French phrase for joy in living

e.note: People will be unsure whether to say it as Joy or as Joey.

e.etymology: An American coinage with no settled meaning, known through champion skateboarder Nyjah Huston.

assoc.t: Nyjah Huston, champion skateboarder

e.etymology: The modern form of the biblical Adaiah, from Hebrew adah, to adorn, and Yah, God. Several Old Testament figures bear it, among them the maternal grandfather of King Josiah.
One of the Cason, Kason and Kayson family of modern American names, built on the -son ending in the pattern of Mason and Jason. Caison also exists as a rare surname of French origin.
A modern name with no settled origin, close in sound to Samara, Tamara and Zamira.
